column2: You will rightly know, in your own nature, the strength and weakness of my rain of words; by that supreme ignorance itself, whose purpose is the destruction of self-interest,
knowledge is attained, O Brahmin, which removes all faults; a weapon is quelled by a weapon, a stain is washed by a stain.
Poison is neutralized by poison, an enemy is slain by an enemy; such is this illusion of beings, which gives joy by its own destruction.
Its nature is not perceived; it perishes just when looked at; "it does not exist in ultimate truth" — contemplate thus with intelligence.
The inner contemplation "all is Brahman" gives liberation; the vision of difference is this ignorance; abandon it wholly.
That state, O sage, is called imperishable, not obtained; let there be no inquiry on your part, O twice-born, "from where was this born?"
Let your inquiry be "how shall I kill it?" When it has set and dwindled, you will know that state.
Whence is this, how is this, how is it destroyed? — in unbroken fashion, make effort for the cure of this house of disease.
So that it will not again bind you in the sorrows of birth. In its own self, by its own vibrations, the clear ocean of consciousness shines.
Contemplate firmly within: "that is one-natured and undivided." The power of consciousness, slightly stirred in the ocean of consciousness,
shines clear, made of it alone, there as a wave in the ocean; in itself, by itself, in space, as the wind in a lake;
so the Self by its own power alone moves about in its own Self; for a moment that goddess shines in the form of all powers.
In whose attainment there is no power of place, time or action, knowing her own nature, though established in the endless state,
she, unperceived, imagines her form as limited; when thus the form is imagined by that supreme beloved,
then follow after her the views of name, number and the like; a form shaped by conceptions, the seat of place, time and action.
This form of consciousness, O Brahmin, is called the knower of the field; he, imagining impressions, again becomes ego.
Egoism is the decider, the stained intellect is called buddhi; the intellect, shaped by intention, goes to the seat of thought.
The mind, dense with conceptions, slowly becomes the senses; the wise know the body, made of hands and feet, and the senses.
Thus the individual, wrapped in the rope of intention and impressions, with a self enveloped in nets of sorrow, gradually comes to lowness.
Thus the mind of the nature of power, having become dense egoism, enters bondage by its own will, like a silkworm in its cocoon.
Dwelling within the net of subtle elements imagined by itself, it falls into utter helplessness like a lion bound in chains.
In one place it is called mind, in another intellect, in another knowledge, in another action, in another egoism, in another thought.
In one place it is called nature, in another imagined as illusion, in another it is called stain, in another remembered as karma.
In one place it is known as bondage, in another recalled as the subtle body of eight, in another called ignorance, in another accepted as desire.
Bearing this whole world that makes the noose of hope, empty of inner fruit like a banyan stripped of seed,
burnt by the flames of the fire of anxiety, chewed by the python of anger, delighting in the waves of the ocean of desire, forgetful of its Self, the grandfather —
lift up the mind, O Brahmin, like an elephant from mud. Thus states resting on the individual, set by contemplation of becoming,
fashioned by Brahma, by the lakh and by the crore, countless, were born before and are still born all around.
And others will be born, like streams of drops from a waterfall; some in their first birth, some beyond a hundred births,
some of countless births, some two or three lives apart; some Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyadharas and great serpents;
some suns, moons, Varunas, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma; some stand as hosts of Brahmins, kings, merchants and servants;
some grasses, herbs, trees, fruits, roots and insects; some Kadamba, Jambira, Sala, Tala and Tamala trees;
some Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mandara and Meru mountains; some oceans of salt, milk, ghee, sugarcane juice;
some vast quarters, some mighty rivers; some in the sky fall and rise high up,
struck unceasingly by death like balls by a hand; having enjoyed thousands of births, again in the strait of the world,
some ignorant fall even after attaining discrimination. The principle of the Self, unlimited by place and time, by its own power
playfully takes a body marked by place and time; that same, through absorption in the impression of individuality, afterwards
becomes the mind, restless, turned toward imagining; the mind-power, imagining, first contemplates in a moment
the pure notion of space, inclined toward the seed and taste of sound; then, gone to density, the mind in the order of dense vibration
contemplates the vibration of air, inclined to the seed and taste of touch; from these two, space and wind, by firm practice,
from the friction of the natures of sound and touch fire is born, together with the subtle element of form, measured with those three.
The mind, gone to such qualities, perceives the subtle element of taste; in a moment it perceives the coolness of waters, from which arises the awareness of water.
Then the mind gone to such qualities contemplates in a moment the subtle element of smell; from this arises the awareness of earth.
Then, enveloped by such subtle elements, giving up thinness, it sees in space a body like a spark of fire, shining.
Joined with a part of egoism, endowed with the seed of intellect, it is called the city of eight, the bee in the lotus of the heart of beings.
In it, by intense emotion, the mind contemplates a radiant body and becomes gross by ripening, like a bilva fruit.
Shining in the clear sky like melted gold in a crucible, that radiance then takes on a form by its own nature.
Above, made of a mass of head; below, made of feet; at the sides arranged with hands; in the middle bearing a belly,
in time becoming distinct, it takes a stainless body, established in intellect, sattva, strength, energy, knowledge and lordship.
He himself is the Lord Brahma, grandfather of all worlds; Brahma, beholding his own lovely excellent body,
the Lord, with spotless sight of the three times, falls to thought: "In this supreme space, in the form of the one Self of pure consciousness,
at the unseen far end, what would be first?" Thus Brahma thought, immediately having the vision of the spotless Self.
He saw groups of creations gone by, many times; then he remembered all, in order of all laws and qualities.
Playfully he imagined by intention various creatures, with varied conduct and undertakings, like a city of Gandharvas.
For them, for heaven and liberation, for the accomplishment of dharma, desire and wealth, he arranged endless varied scriptures.
Because it is imagined by the mind in the form of Virinchi, the world's continuance is declared to last that long; when that is destroyed, it would be destroyed.
Nothing is ever born or dies anywhere at any time; in ultimate truth, O best of Brahmins, all that is seen is false.
Abandon the sheath of the serpents of hope, the pomp of the world; knowing "this is unreal," settle in the attitude of a mother.
For a city of Gandharvas, adorned or unadorned, or in a portion of ignorance, sons and the like — what order is there of pleasure and pain?
When wealth and wives increase there is pain, not contentment; when the illusion of delusion grows, who here has comfort?
By the same things by which attachment arises in the fool, grown strong, by those same portions dispassion arises in the wise.
Therefore, Nidagha, knower of truth, in the dealings of the world, ignore what is lost, lost; take what is obtained, obtained.
Natural non-wishing for pleasures not yet come, and for those that come, enjoyment —
having understood and relying on the pure state between existence and non-existence, do not grasp the seen, outer and inner, and do not reject it.
He whose desire and non-desire are alike, the knower abiding in action — his insight is not tainted, like a lotus leaf by water.
If the splendor of sense-objects does not stir in your heart, O twice-born, then, having known the knowable, you have crossed the ocean of becoming.
For the high state, by supreme insight separate the mind's modification from the host of impressions, as one removes scent from a flower.
In this ocean of the world flooded with the water of impressions, those who have climbed the boat of knowledge are crossed over — the supreme wise.
Those who know both shores neither abandon nor wish for dealings in the world; they follow all of it.
Of the infinite principle of the Self, of the form of common being, the turning of consciousness toward the perceived is known as the sprout of intention.
That which has obtained a trace of being slowly becomes dense, filling out mindhood firmly, for dullness, like a cloud.
They contemplate the perceived as if separate from consciousness itself; it becomes like intention, like a seed becoming a sprout.
Intention itself is born of itself and grows quickly of itself, for sorrow and not for happiness.
Do not form intentions; do not contemplate a notion in what stands; strive for the destruction of intention, after which it does not follow again.
By mere non-contemplation, intention dwindles of itself; cutting intention with intention itself, O sage, the mind with the mind,
stay in your own Self; what is difficult in this? As this sky is void, so indeed is the world void.
As the husk of rice and the blackness of copper are destroyed by action, O Brahmin, so is the stain of a person.
The stain of the individual, like that of rice, though innate, is also destroyed without doubt; therefore be energetic.
Giving up inner reliance on the glory of notions made of contemplation, whoever you are, you are; wander playfully in this world, sinless one.
By this firm contemplation "everywhere I am a non-doer," that evenness named supreme nectar alone remains.
In sorrow, joy and sport, by seeing oneself alone as doer, when one's own intention is destroyed, evenness alone remains.
That evenness in all states, which is the supreme true condition — the mind abiding in it does not again take birth.
Or, O sage, giving up both all-doership and non-doership, drinking up the mind, whoever you are, you are; be steady.
Steady in the remainder and in concentration, give up that by which you give up; the form of consciousness and mind's imagining, light and darkness and the like.
Impressions and the one who is impressed, preceded by the vibration of life-breath, abandoning all with its root, equal to the sky, of quiet mind,
abandoning from the heart all rows of impressions, he who stays free of agitation is liberated, the Supreme Lord.
All that is seen and to be seen is wandering; by delusion the ten directions; for the wise one acting with reason, the world has the shape of a cow's hoofprint.
In the body, outer and inner, below, above and in all directions, here the Self, there too the Self; there is no world made of the non-Self.
There is nothing where I am not; there is nothing not made of it; what else would I wish for? All is spread out, made of being-consciousness.
All this is indeed Brahman; all this is spread out as the Self; abandon, sinless one, the delusion "I am one, this is another."
In the extended, dense Brahman, eternal, imagined things do not arise; there is no grief, no delusion, no old age or birth.
What exists here, that alone exists; be free of fever always; by experiencing what comes as it comes, by not longing anywhere.
Renouncing giving up and taking, be free of fever always; for whoever has this last birth, O great-minded, to him swiftly
pure knowledge enters, like a pearl into the best bamboo; this has been declared by one's own experience for those of dispassionate mind.
From the union of the seer with the seen arises the certainty of the delight of cognition; we worship that unvibrating one that arises from the principle of one's own Self.
Giving up seer, seeing and seen together with impressions, we worship the Self that appears as the cognition of seeing.
We worship the Self, ever in the middle of the two sides "it is" and "it is not," the illuminator of lights.
Those who abandon the god, the Lord in the cave of the heart, and go to another, seek a jewel having thrown away the Kaustubha in hand.
One should strike these enemies, the senses, again and again, whether risen or not risen, with the staff of discrimination, as Hari struck the mountains with the thunderbolt.
In the bad dream of the night of the world, in the void delusion made of the body, all that seen is impure — the confusion of worldly existence.
